en_summary: @firesidealpha: Ray Dalio says investors mistake great technology for a great investment in a bubble and compares the AI boom with the innovations of the 1920s. Bubble is not just price beyond PV of future cash flows because future cash flows unknown for decades.
text:
Ray Dalio says investors mistake great technology for a great investment in a bubble and compares the AI boom with the innovations of the 1920s

“A lot of people think a bubble is whether the price gets beyond that which can come from the present value of future cash flows, and that’s not it, because what happens is you don’t know the future cash flows for decades, let’s say, if you take the present value.

“In any case, even those with good financial cash flows have had bubbles. So you could see the 1920s bubbles, and then you have the collapses. Even if they work out in the long run, you have the bubble bursting.

“The bubble, the mechanics of it, is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment.

“In the ’20s, imagine what that was like. That was the first time you had electricity in houses, so you had lighting and you had refrigeration. You had movies, you had radio, you had cars, you had airplanes—all of this new technology coming on. It would be more apparent than anything we’ve seen even with AI.”

text:
Who could buy Penguin Solutions, and at what price? $PENG 

1. $SKHY — The obvious one.

Its US AI investment arm, HYAICO, holds convertible preferred stock equal to 9.1% of Penguin. It paid $377m for a stake SK Telecom bought for $200m in 2024, in a transfer inside SK Group. HYAICO has up to $10bn to deploy in US AI companies. The two companies have worked together on AI data centers since January 2025, and the stake comes with board nomination rights.

The logic: Penguin is now mostly a memory business, and it builds and runs the AI clusters that memory goes into. For a memory maker that is a customer, a channel and a window into demand.

The catch: the investor agreement includes a standstill on buying more shares and a requirement to vote with Penguin's board. SK hynix cannot creep to control. A deal would have to be friendly and negotiated.

2. $DELL

Dell sells AI servers at huge scale and wants more of the services and software that sit on top. Penguin has years of experience running large GPU clusters and its own cluster-management software. Buying that is faster than building it.

3. $HPE

Same logic, and arguably a closer fit: HPE's heritage is high-performance computing, which is where Penguin came from.

The catch for both: I know of no reporting of interest, and any buyer has to deal with SK hynix's investor rights first.

4. $MRVL

Penguin is working with Marvell on CXL and photonic memory. Partners sometimes become owners.

The catch: chip designers rarely want

text:
Steve Eisman reveals he shorted roughly half his Nvidia holding against his long position before Jensen was reinstated, and says he hedged much of his technology portfolio months ago

Steven Bartlett: “What are you investing in in this moment? I’ve been thinking a lot about this.”

Steve Eisman: “I had a lot of the technology companies in my portfolio, and about four months or so, I shorted most of them against the box to reduce my risk.”

Steven Bartlett: “You shorted most of them against the box? What does that mean?”

Steve Eisman: “Let’s say I own 100 shares of Nvidia, just make up a number, and I’ve owned it for a very long time. And I’m nervous. The problem is, if I sell my Nvidia, I’ve got to pay massive taxes on the gain. And I don’t want to do that, unless I’m so freaked out that I’ll do it anyway. You’re talking about 30%, 35% taxes. It’s a lot.

“So what you can do for a time, you can’t do it forever, is I can short 50 shares or 75 shares or even 100 shares of Nvidia. So now my Nvidia exposure is a lot lower.

“If I were to do that today, I’d have to cover the entire position at the end of January. That’s just the way the tax rules work. But during that period, I wouldn’t have any real exposure to Nvidia. That’s what I did.”

Steven Bartlett: “So you’re shorting Nvidia?”

Steve Eisman: “Well, I’m long it, and I shorted like half of my position.”

en_summary: Applied Optoelectronics $AAOI locked in a second hyperscaler. The 2027 piece alone is about two-thirds of what the Street expects AOI to sell next year. Signed a multiyear agreement with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer. Mentions $ANET $COHR $FN $LITE $NVDA.
text:
Applied Optoelectronics $AAOI just locked in a second hyperscaler, and the 2027 piece alone is about two-thirds of what the Street expects AOI to sell next year.

AOI signed a multiyear agreement with an existing Tier-1 hyperscale datacenter customer running from December 2026 through December 2030. The customer committed to buy about $1.5B of 800G transceivers in 2027 and about $0.7B of laser diodes in 2028 and 2029, so $2.2B in minimum commitments. For scale, AOI's total 2027 revenue is at $2.26B market consensus. AOI is covering a $2M one-time expense to speed up qualification, and the customer put in no capital.

The bigger number comes with an asterisk. "While not guaranteed, the current level of demand based on long-term discussions with the customer exceeds $10 billion over the four years of the LTA," said CFO Stefan Murry. Anything beyond the $2.2B depends on AOI bringing capacity online and winning more purchase commitments.

The detail I like most: AOI expects some of those laser diodes to power co-packaged optics starting in 2028, and it plans to expand laser manufacturing in Texas. It also committed to ship an agreed amount of product made in the USA starting in Q1 2027 and ramping through the year.

Why it matters: optics is one of the tightest parts of the AI buildout, and hyperscalers are now locking in multi-year supply the way they have for memory. AOI's problem has been capacity, with power delaying part of its US expansion and two ATM programs totaling $1.1
